_about: Single source for the page's people-centred content: proto-personas, journeys and service blueprints, worked examples, tutorials, user guide, hints, toolkit, ways to get involved and the guided tour. tools/build-site.mjs renders the page sections, docs/user-guide.md and docs/toolkit/* from this file and stops the build if a reference does not resolve. Everything about people here is an assumption to be tested with real users (open item O-03).
status: Proto-personas and assumed journeys. Written from the tools, the standard and the people this kind of service usually serves; not yet tested in research with real users (open item O-03).

personas.context: Publishes datasets for an organisation to data.gov.uk, often alongside another job.
personas.goal: Get records complete and correct before a return, an audit or a release, without learning the whole standard first.
pains: Finds out which attributes are required only when something is rejected
Catalogue fields and xGov MEM attributes have different names
No quick way to see what a record still lacks
personas.contributes: Tells us where a verdict disagrees with the standard or with how records are really kept.
personas.champions: Shares the metadata readiness checklist with other publishers.

personas.context: Answers questions with data and needs to know quickly what exists, who holds it and whether it can be reused.
personas.goal: Find candidate datasets, judge whether they are fit for the question, and cite them properly.
pains: Keyword search returns many near-duplicates
Licence, update frequency and format are buried
Hard to tell a maintained dataset from an abandoned one
personas.contributes: Suggests searches that went badly so the tool descriptions and results can improve.
personas.champions: Shares the prompt library with their analysis community.

personas.context: Looks after metadata quality across an organisation or a community of publishers.
personas.goal: See how far records are from xGov MEM, find the common gaps, and explain the standards in plain terms.
pains: Conformance is checked by hand, one record at a time
Colleagues ask what a standard is for and where it stands
Business terms are drafted in many places with no record of review
personas.contributes: Checks validation against their own records and reports disagreements with the model.
personas.champions: Runs the show-and-tell and the co-design session in their community.

personas.context: Connects tools to assistants, agents or pipelines and has to answer for what they do.
personas.goal: Add data discovery and metadata checks to an assistant safely, with predictable inputs and no side effects.
pains: Needs to know exactly what each tool reads and returns
Must show that nothing writes, sends or stores data
Wants to try tools before wiring them in
personas.contributes: Opens pull requests with tests, and reports defects with a way to reproduce them.
personas.champions: Shows other builders how the server is checked: the defect register and its checks.

personas.context: Not a data specialist. Uses an AI assistant to understand what data exists and what the standards mean.
personas.goal: Get a plain-English answer they can trust, with a link to the source they can pass on.
pains: Jargon: DCAT, CURIE, crosswalk
Cannot tell whether an assistant's answer came from a real source
Does not know who to ask
personas.contributes: Tells us where an answer was unclear, so explanations and the glossary improve.
personas.champions: Points colleagues at the glossary and the worked examples.

personas.context: Promotes good data practice inside their organisation, usually on top of a day job.
personas.goal: Show colleagues something useful in under an hour and leave them able to carry on alone.
pains: Little time to prepare material
Needs examples that work on the day
Hard to collect feedback in a form others can act on
personas.contributes: Collects feedback from sessions and raises it through the contact form.
personas.champions: Uses the champion pack and the session plan from the toolkit.

personas.context: Wants to shape the service: report, test, suggest, design or code.
personas.goal: Make a change that is accepted, and see what happened to their idea.
pains: Unclear where ideas go and how they are decided
Worried a change will be rejected on process
No visible roadmap
personas.contributes: Joins co-design sessions, improves the standards list, writes tests and checks.
personas.champions: Brings a second organisation's view, so the work is not shaped by one.

examples.title: Check a record before it goes out
examples.situation: A Dataset record is ready to publish, but two attributes were never filled in.
examples.prompt: Check this Dataset record against xGov MEM and list anything I must fix before I publish it: <paste the record>
examples.check: Each finding names the attribute path. Fix the errors; consider the warnings.

examples.title: Catch a misspelt attribute
examples.situation: The record uses US spelling for one attribute name, so the model does not recognise it and treats the real attribute as missing.
examples.prompt: Validate this record and tell me if any attribute names are not in the model: <paste the record>
examples.check: Look for an unknown attribute and a missing one with a similar name together: that pair usually means a spelling difference.

examples.title: Spot a value outside the allowed list
examples.situation: Access rights were typed by hand and do not match one of the model's values.
examples.prompt: Check this record and, for any value outside the model's list, show me the allowed values: <paste the record>
examples.check: Choose one of the allowed values exactly as written, including capital letters.

examples.title: What could connect UK Export Finance and HMRC?
examples.situation: An export finance team wants to check exporters and size markets using HMRC's published APIs, before asking for any restricted data.
examples.prompt: Find HMRC APIs that could help an export finance team check an exporter's VAT and EORI numbers and size a market for a product. For each, give the documentation link, how access works, and whether it is in the government API catalogue.
examples.check: Open each documentation link before relying on it. Customs declarations about a named trader are not open APIs: they need a legal gateway and a data-sharing agreement.

examples.title: Find data on a topic
examples.situation: You need recent data on a topic and want the licence and format before you open anything.
examples.prompt: Search data.gov.uk for road traffic counts. Show the ten most relevant results as a table with title, publisher, licence, formats and last updated, and give me each catalogue link.
examples.check: Results change as the catalogue changes, so none are shown here. Open the catalogue link before you rely on a result.

examples.title: See how ready a catalogue entry is for xGov MEM
examples.situation: You want to know what a real catalogue entry would still need to meet the model.
examples.prompt: Describe the data.gov.uk dataset <name or id> and list the xGov MEM attributes its record still lacks, required ones first.
examples.check: Missing attributes are reported as missing, never guessed. Compare with the real-record sample on this page.

examples.title: Explain a standard to a colleague
examples.situation: A colleague asks what Open Referral UK is for and whether it is current.
examples.prompt: Explain Open Referral UK in plain English: what it is for, its status, its licence and where to read it. Tell me how sure you are of each fact.
examples.check: Each answer carries a provenance label and a check date. Anything not verified at the primary source should be re-read there.

examples.title: Check whether a business term is certified
examples.situation: A term is used in a report and you need to know who defined it and whether it was reviewed.
examples.prompt: Look up the term 'crosswalk'. Who drafted it, what review level has it passed, and is it certified?
examples.check: A term counts as certified only when it is endorsed after review at level H2 or above. Anything unrecorded is reported as unknown.

examples.title: Find tools that work alongside this one
examples.situation: You want to know which other servers cover data quality or related jobs.
examples.prompt: List the MCP servers that work alongside this one, what each is for, and where each manifest came from.
examples.check: This server lists the others but never calls them. Each entry names the repository and commit its manifest came from.

examples.title: Find an MCP server for UK legislation
examples.situation: You want an assistant that can also look up legislation, and want to know what servers exist and whether any is endorsed.
examples.prompt: Which MCP servers could I use alongside this one for UK legislation? Tell me each one's status and where it was checked.
examples.check: Candidates are listed for review only and are not endorsed. Read each server's own documentation and safety statement before connecting it.

tutorials.title: Check your first record in two minutes, with nothing to install
steps: Go to Check a record on this page.
Choose the example called 'Two required attributes missing'. The record appears in the box.
Leave Class as 'Work it out from the record' and select Check the record.
Read the findings. Each one names the attribute and whether it is an error (must fix) or a warning (recommended).
Now paste one of your own records, as JSON. Nothing you paste leaves your browser.
Fix the errors in your source system, not here: this checker only reads.

tutorials.title: Install the server and connect your assistant
steps: Check you have Node.js 20 or later: run node --version.
Clone, install and build with the four commands in Quick start.
Add the server to your assistant using the snippet for Claude Desktop or VS Code. Replace the path with where you cloned it.
Restart the assistant. It should list the tools in the data dictionary.
Not working? Run npm run inspector and call a tool by hand. If it works there, the problem is the assistant's settings.
Ask: 'Which standards can you explain?' The answer should come from standard_explain.

tutorials.title: Fix a catalogue record from start to finish
steps: Pick one record you are responsible for. Note its data.gov.uk name or id.
Ask your assistant to describe it and list what its xGov MEM record lacks (worked example: See how ready a catalogue entry is).
Download the Dataset record template and the readiness checklist from the toolkit.
Fill the gaps from the people who hold the facts. Do not invent values: an empty gap is better than a wrong one.
Validate the finished record with metadata_validate or the in-page checker until there are no errors.
Update the record in your own catalogue. This server never writes anywhere.
After the catalogue next harvests, describe the record again to confirm the gaps have closed.

tutorials.title: Make a first contribution: add or correct a standard
steps: Read the contributing guide and fork the repository.
Open src/data/standards.json. Each entry has a name, purpose, status, licence, link, provenance label and check date.
Read the standard at its primary source. Set the provenance to V only if you checked it there, with today's date; otherwise use S, K or U.
Run npm run verify. It rebuilds the page and runs every check.
Open a pull request explaining what you checked and where.
The maintainer reviews it. If it is merged, the page updates on the next build.

tutorials.title: Run a 45-minute show-and-tell
steps: Download the session plan and the champion pack from the toolkit.
Before the session, run each worked example you plan to show, so you know what to expect.
Open with the problem, not the tool: ask who has had a record rejected or could not find data.
Show the in-page checker live. It needs no install and no network.
Let people try one of their own records, in pairs.
Close with the feedback questions, then raise what you heard through the contact form.

items.q: Do I need to install anything to try it?
items.a: No. The record checker on this page runs the server's own validator in your browser. To use the tools from an assistant, you need to install the server.

items.q: What do I need to install it?
items.a: Node.js 20 or later, git, and an assistant that supports MCP, such as Claude Desktop or VS Code.
Any assistant that can start an MCP server over stdio. Snippets are given for Claude Desktop and VS Code; others follow the same pattern.

items.q: How do I choose a tool?
items.a: You usually do not: ask your question and the assistant picks. To be sure, name the tool in your prompt, for example 'use metadata_validate'.

items.q: Can I check many records at once?
items.a: Each call checks one record. Ask the assistant to go through a list and give you a table, then check the totals yourself.

items.q: Why do I see at most 100 findings?
items.a: Findings are capped at 100 per call, with a count of how many were left out, so one very broken record cannot flood the reply (defect D-020).

items.q: Can I point it at a different catalogue or vocabulary?
items.a: Yes. NDL_MCP_CKAN_BASE sets the catalogue API (https only) and NDL_MCP_VOCAB_PATH sets the vocabulary term_lookup reads. See the README for details.

items.q: Does it call the APIs it finds?
items.a: No. api_search and server_search list APIs and servers with where each entry came from; this server never calls them, holds no keys and passes no data.
No. Every tool is read-only. It never writes to a catalogue, sends messages or stores what you ask.
No personal data is read or returned. Do not paste personal data into the checker or your prompts.

items.q: Can I rely on the answers?
items.a: Results come from the sources named with them, but the assistant can still make mistakes. Check the source before you rely on a result, and treat provenance labels S, K and U as leads, not facts.
No. It is an independent prototype. It is not endorsed by any government department and does not set policy.

items.q: The assistant does not show the tools
items.a: Check the path in the settings points at dist/index.js, that npm run build finished, and restart the assistant. Then try npm run inspector.
The catalogue may be unreachable. A weekly live smoke test watches for changes to its API; check the open items, then raise it through the contact form.

items.q: The checker says my record is invalid, but I think it is right
items.a: Check the class is right and attribute names are spelt as the model spells them (UK spelling, for example licence). If you still disagree, tell us: it may be a difference from the standard.

tips.tip: Name the tool in your prompt when you need a specific one.
Ask for a table with the catalogue link in every row, so each answer can be checked.
Ask the assistant to say how sure it is, and which tool each fact came from.
Use api_search to check whether an API already exists before you build or buy one.
Use organisation, limit and offset with catalogue_search to page through one publisher's records.
A missing attribute next to an unknown one with a similar name is usually a spelling difference.
Values in the model's lists are exact, including capitals: OPEN, not Open.
Record the model commit shown with the results whenever you report conformance.
Cite the catalogue entry, not the assistant.
Keep the validated JSON next to the change you make in your own catalogue.
Use the in-page checker for live demos: it needs no network.
